subject: Business
title: Peak-End Rule: How Experiences Are Remembered
description: A micro-lesson that makes Peak-End Rule: How Experiences Are Remembered usable.

hook.text: A 60-minute pleasant flight with turbulence at landing is remembered worse than a 60-minute rough flight with a smooth.

buildup.text: Daniel Kahneman's peak-end rule: we judge experiences by their most intense moment and how they end.

discovery.text: The total duration barely matters. A long wait with a great ending beats a short wait with a bad one.

twist.text: Most businesses optimize the beginning of experiences. The peak-end rule says the ending matters more.

climax.text: IKEA's cheap ice cream at the exit reframes a stressful shopping trip. The last moment wins.

punchline.text: Nail the ending. That's what people actually remember.

quiz.question: According to the peak-end rule, how do people judge experiences?
options: By the most intense moment and how the experience ends
By the total duration of the experience

details.summary: The peak-end rule, discovered by Daniel Kahneman, shows that people judge experiences based primarily on the most intense moment and the final moment rather than the average of the entire experience. This means how an experience ends disproportionately shapes overall memory and satisfaction.
details.whyItMatters: Customer experience design should focus resources on creating memorable peak moments and strong endings rather than uniformly improving every touchpoint. The peak-end rule explains why a great dessert can redeem an average meal.
takeaways: People judge experiences by their peak intensity and how they ended
A strong ending can salvage a mediocre overall experience in customer memory
Duration of an experience has surprisingly little impact on how it is remembered

faq.question: How can businesses apply the peak-end rule to customer experience?
faq.answer: Design memorable positive moments during the experience peak. End interactions on a high note with unexpected gifts, personal touches, or warm goodbyes. Front-load unpleasant steps like paperwork and end with enjoyable ones. Disney parks engineer peak moments and magical endings.

faq.question: Does the peak-end rule apply to negative experiences too?
faq.answer: Yes. A painful medical procedure ending with less pain is remembered as less unpleasant overall even if total pain was greater. Customer service that resolves a complaint with an unexpected bonus creates positive memories despite the initial negative experience that prompted the call.
